entries.answer: Panoorin is the Tagalog verb for to watch, and it is the ordinary word for watching a film, a show or a match. Its object marker changes what it takes: panoorin ang TV is direct, and a specific thing being watched usually takes a linker, so panoorin ng Baywatch and panoorin ito mean slightly different things to a speaker. It is a reflexive form, built on panoorin itself, so the verb in a sentence is panoorin or pinapanood depending on the tense. The word is not restricted to a screen, so panoorin ang mga salamin, meaning to look at them, is a different sense that a learner meets immediately. A related verb is manood, which is a synonym used in a few regions, and pakinggan is the equivalent for listening, so the two together are what a person uses for media.

entries.answer: YouTube is a video platform, and the Filipino word for it is usually the name itself, since the company name is used untranslated the way it is in most languages. A Filipino speaker says watching YouTube for watching a video, usually in a compound, and the same word names the app and the act. What people use it for has moved over time: it began as a place for uploaded clips and became a general video library, which is why it now holds a mixture of music, film clips, tutorials, and long personal commentary. The practical advice for anyone choosing what to watch is that the most-searched thing is not the most worth watching, because the algorithm promotes what keeps someone watching rather than what is good, so a recommendation is more useful than a search there. The same is true of short-form video, where the length of a clip and the length of the attention are the same thing.
